..
Issued at 336 AM CST Fri Nov 20 2026

Surface high pressure over the Appalachians has helped maintain 
light south/southeasterly winds through the overnight, with high 
clouds being the only weather of note as temperatures dip into the 
mid-to-upper 40s/low 50s areawide. Upper ridging continues to 
progress eastward as an upper trough over the West Coast digs 
towards the Intermountain West, with a shortwave lifting from the 
Intermountain West towards the Dakotas. A lee cyclone developing in 
conjunction with the passing trough will enhance the surface 
pressure gradient across the Central Plains. This in turn will bring 
winds back up across the forecast area to 15-25 mph, with deep 
boundary layer mixing aiding in mixing down higher winds and 
allowing gusts up to 25-35 mph. Higher winds will be present further 
to the north and west, closer to the greatest surface pressure 
gradient and highest winds aloft with the passing shortwave. 
Temperatures will continue to warm through the day as southerly flow 
and subsequent WAA is reinforced across the area, with highs in the 
high 60s across much of the forecast area and low-to-mid 70s across 
primarily central MO. Although high winds and warm temperatures 
would promote a critical fire weather setup, greater moisture 
transport in the low-levels will mitigate critical conditions by 
increasing minimum relative humidity. However, with the 
aforementioned high winds and warm temperatures, burning still may 
not be the best idea.

As the surface cyclone lifts off towards the northeast, a cold 
frontal boundary will begin to sag southeastward from the northern 
Plains. The western trough will continue progressing towards the 
east, with weak cyclogenesis over the southern Plains reinforcing 
southerly flow into the central Plains during the day Saturday. This 
will continue to promote greater warm/moist advection in the low-
levels towards the forecast area out ahead of the cold front, and 
allow daytime highs to remain in the high 60s/low-to-mid 70s. As the 
cold front continues to progress southeastward, a line of 
showers/thunderstorms will develop along the cold front by Saturday 
evening, pushing from the northwest towards the southeast overnight. 
As has been the case for the past several forecast cycles, the 
environment is characterized by high effective shear and low CAPE 
out ahead of the cold front. This continues to place some 
uncertainty on the severity of activity as it develops during the 
evening and into the overnight, especially as greater CIN builds and 
activity becomes more elevated in nature. With high effective shear 
and the presence of at least marginal CAPE in the atmosphere, strong 
thunderstorms are not entirely out of the question, with hazards of 
strong winds/small hail if storms can fully realize the environment. 
However, with more factors working against severe activity rather 
than for it, this potential remains brief and low. 

As the cold front fully moves through by Sunday, temperatures will 
drop into the 40s/50s as surface high pressure builds in from the 
north alongside upper ridging from the west. This will allow the 
forecast through the early half of next week to remain cooler and 
drier, with progressively north/northeasterly flow in the low-levels 
pushing daytime highs down solidly into the 40s and overnight lows 
below freezing. Behind the upper ridge, synoptic guidance is 
increasingly converging on the progression of an upper trough from 
the West Coast towards the east, with another trough digging down 
from the Canadian Interior Plains. The exact evolution of the 
synoptic environment looks to remain dependent on the interaction of 
these two troughs and how they progress relative to the departing 
upper ridge. However, regardless of individual solution, weather 
looks to remain generally cool and dry for the forecast area through 
the remainder of the forecast period.
